titleEn: Why have You rejected us for ever?
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | Bb A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty-three verses of communal lament written after a sanctuary has been burned. It is not one of the seven daily psalms; it is what a community says when a building it thought permanent is gone and nobody can say how long the silence will last. Two things to watch. The second person singular suffix, -cha, Your, sits on almost every noun the psalm names: Your congregation, Your inheritance, Your meeting place, Your sanctuary, Your name, so that every loss is stated as God's loss before it is stated as the speaker's. And from verse 13 to verse 17 the word for You opens six clauses in a row, each with a verb in the perfect. The middle of the psalm is a list of things already done, laid out as an argument for doing them again.

stichs.en: A maskil of Asaph.
Why, O God, have You rejected us for ever?
Why does Your anger smoke against the flock of Your pasture?

verses.summary: The opening is a question about duration, not about the event. Nothing is described yet, and already the sheep are called God's own property rather than the speaker's.

stichs.en: Remember Your congregation, which You acquired long ago,
which You redeemed as the tribe of Your inheritance,
Mount Zion, this place where You dwelt.

verses.summary: One imperative and three objects, each attached to a different verb of acquisition: bought, redeemed, lived in. The argument is ownership, not pity.

stichs.en: Lift up Your steps to the everlasting ruins,
to all the harm the enemy has done in the sanctuary.

verses.summary: The prayer asks God to walk to the site and look. Ruins called perpetual are ruins nobody in the community expects to see rebuilt.

stichs.en: Your foes have roared inside Your meeting place;
they have set up their own standards as signs.

verses.summary: Noise replaces liturgy. The same word covers both what the enemy plants and what used to mark the appointed times, so the substitution is exact.

stichs.en: It looked like men swinging on high,
axes in a thicket of trees.

verses.summary: The Hebrew here is broken and every translation of it is a reconstruction. What survives intact is the sound: axes working in a wood.

stichs.en: And now its carved work, all of it together,
they smash down with hatchet and hammers.

verses.summary: The verse names the tools. Panelling that took years to carve comes down in an afternoon of ordinary demolition work.

stichs.en: They have set Your sanctuary on fire;
they have profaned the dwelling of Your name to the ground.

verses.summary: Two losses, and the second is the heavier one. A building can be rebuilt; what has been emptied is the place where the name was said to live.

stichs.en: They said in their heart: let us crush them all together;
they burned every meeting place of God in the land.

verses.summary: The enemy speaks once in the whole psalm, and what comes out is policy rather than rage: complete, and applied everywhere in the country.

stichs.en: We do not see our own signs;
there is no prophet any more,
and there is nobody with us who knows how long.

verses.summary: The sharpest loss is not the building. It is that no one is left who can date the end, so the grief has no measurable edge.

stichs.en: How long, O God, will the foe taunt?
Will the enemy revile Your name for ever?

verses.summary: The second question of the psalm. The concern has moved off the flock and onto the name, which is the ground the petition will later stand on.

stichs.en: Why do You draw back Your hand, Your right hand?
Out of the fold of Your garment, make an end of it.

verses.summary: A hand tucked into the fold of a garment is a picture of chosen inaction. The last word of the verse turns the complaint into an order.

stichs.en: Yet God is my King from of old,
working acts of deliverance in the middle of the earth.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. Complaint stops here and the recitation begins, and the possessive turns personal for the first time: my King.

stichs.en: You broke the sea apart by Your strength;
You shattered the heads of the sea monsters on the waters.

verses.summary: The first of six clauses that open with the word You. All the verbs are perfect: this is a record being entered as evidence.

stichs.en: You crushed the heads of Leviathan;
You gave him as food to a people, to the creatures of the desert.

verses.summary: The monster is not simply killed. The carcass is handed out, so that even the most violent line in the psalm ends in provision for somebody.

stichs.en: You split open spring and torrent;
You dried up rivers that never run dry.

verses.summary: One power running in both directions: water opened where there was none, water stopped where it had always run. Neither state is fixed against God.

stichs.en: Yours is the day, Yours also the night;
You established the light and the sun.

verses.summary: The argument steps down from sea monsters to the ordinary alternation of day and night, which is a harder thing to doubt and therefore a stronger claim.

stichs.en: You fixed all the boundaries of the earth;
summer and winter, You formed them.

verses.summary: The last of the You clauses is about reliability, which is precisely what the ruined sanctuary has put in question. The list ends where the wound is.

stichs.en: Remember this: an enemy has taunted the LORD,
and a vile people have reviled Your name.

verses.summary: The petition resumes with the imperative of verse 2, but the object has changed. What is to be remembered now is the insult, not the congregation.

stichs.en: Do not hand the life of Your dove to the wild beast;
do not forget the life of Your poor for ever.

verses.summary: Two negative imperatives around two fragile lives. The exact syntax of the first line is disputed, but the pairing of dove and poor is clear enough.

stichs.en: Look to the covenant,
for the dark places of the land are full of the haunts of violence.

verses.summary: The covenant is produced as the legal ground of the request. The dark places are described as inhabited, which is worse than describing them as empty.

stichs.en: Do not let the crushed turn back humiliated;
let the poor and the needy praise Your name.

verses.summary: The one verse that asks for something on behalf of a person rather than a building. The outcome requested is praise, which is what the sanctuary was for.

stichs.en: Arise, O God, plead Your own case;
remember the reproach You take from a vile man all day long.

verses.summary: God is asked to litigate on His own behalf. The reproach is called God's, not Israel's, which is the argument the whole psalm has been assembling.

stichs.en: Do not forget the voice of Your foes,
the uproar of those who rise against You, going up without stop.

verses.summary: It ends on the sound it started describing in verse 4, still rising. No answer is given and no resolution is written in.

pardes.body: Three movements. Verses 1 to 11 say what happened and ask two questions, why and how long. {{12.0}} turns the psalm: God is named King and the tense shifts from complaint to record. Verses 13 to 17 list what God has already done, six clauses each opening with {{13.0}}. Verses 18 to 23 are the petition, built almost entirely of imperatives: remember, look, arise, and twice do not forget. Watch one word travel the whole text. The word for perpetuity or for ever stands at {{1.5}}, {{3.3}}, {{10.8}} and {{19.9}}: it is what the speaker fears about the rejection, what the ruins are called, what the insult threatens to become, and the last thing God is asked not to do.

Verses 5 and 6 are among the most damaged in the book. Verse 5 does not parse cleanly in Hebrew and every rendering of it, including the one on this page, is a reconstruction; {{5.5}}, axes, is the one word nobody argues about. {{8.2}} is equally obscure and is usually read from a root meaning to oppress or to crush. The crux for dating the psalm is {{9.5}}: a text that says there is no prophet any more sits either after 586 BCE, when the Temple was burned, or in the Maccabean crisis, when the sanctuary was desecrated but not destroyed. Both dates are argued and neither is settled. {{14.3}} is the sea monster of Canaanite myth, and the psalm treats it as something already dealt with rather than as a threat.

The imperative {{2.0}}, remember, is aimed at God three times here, and twice more in the negative form, do not forget. It is never aimed at the congregation. The human side of this psalm is presented as having nothing left to do except remind. A long-standing reading takes the giving of Leviathan as food in verse 14 as a feast for the righteous at the end of days, which turns the most violent verse in the psalm into a promise. {{19.4}}, Your dove, is widely read as a name for Israel and the wild beast opposite it as whichever empire is current, and that pairing is what let the psalm be reused after every later destruction instead of only the first.

The six You clauses of verses 13 to 17 are all acts of separation: sea broken from land, springs opened, rivers stopped, day divided from night, summer from winter, boundaries set around the earth. In the kabbalistic idiom that is creation described as the drawing of limits, and the burned sanctuary is then the one limit that has failed. Asking God to remember is not a request for information in this reading but the standard movement of arousal from below: the human side acts by speaking, and the covenant of {{20.1}} is held up as the document that obliges the other side to answer.
